title: Periodicity
lead: The representative elements divide into metals, metalloids and nonmetals by their places in the periodic table. The representative metals are taken group by group, from the alkali metals through groups 2, 12, 13 and 14 to bismuth in group 15, with how readily each reacts, the ions each forms and the films that protect them.
objectives: Make predictions about the periodicity properties of the representative elements
summary_html: This section focuses on the periodicity of the representative elements. These are the elements where the electrons are entering the s and p orbitals. The representative elements occur in groups 1, 2, and 12–18. These elements are representative metals, metalloids, and nonmetals. The alkali metals (group 1) are very reactive, readily form ions with a charge of 1+ to form ionic compounds that are usually soluble in water, and react vigorously with water to form hydrogen gas and a basic solution of the metal hydroxide. The outermost electrons of the alkaline earth metals (group 2) are more difficult to remove than the outer electron of the alkali metals, leading to the group 2 metals being less reactive than those in group 1. These elements easily form compounds in which the metals exhibit an oxidation state of 2+. Zinc, cadmium, and mercury (group 12) commonly exhibit the group oxidation state of 2+ (although mercury also exhibits an oxidation state of 1+ in compounds that contain ${\text{Hg}}_{2}{}^{2+}).$ Aluminum, gallium, indium, and thallium (group 13) are easier to oxidize than is hydrogen. Aluminum, gallium, and indium occur with an oxidation state 3+ (however, thallium also commonly occurs as the Tl+ ion). Tin and lead form stable divalent cations and covalent compounds in which the metals exhibit the 4+-oxidation state.

exercises.prompt: How do alkali metals differ from alkaline earth metals in atomic structure and general properties?

answer.solution: The alkali metals all have a single s electron in their outermost shell. In contrast, the alkaline earth metals have a completed s subshell in their outermost shell. In general, the alkali metals react faster and are more reactive than the corresponding alkaline earth metals in the same period.

exercises.prompt: Why does the reactivity of the alkali metals decrease from cesium to lithium?

answer.solution: Reactivity falls from cesium to lithium because the single valence electron is held more tightly in each lighter atom. Every alkali metal reacts by losing its one ns1 electron to form a 1+ ion, so the metal that gives up that electron most easily is the most readily oxidized and the most reactive. Moving up the group from cesium to lithium, the atoms have fewer electron shells and are smaller, so the valence electron lies closer to the nucleus and is less shielded from it. The attraction it feels grows, and the first ionization energy rises from about 376 kJ/mol for cesium to about 520 kJ/mol for lithium. With more energy needed to remove the electron, lithium is the least readily oxidized and least reactive of these metals, while cesium, losing its electron most easily, is the most reactive.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the formulas for the nine compounds that may form when each species in column 1 of the table reacts with each species in column 2.
12
NaI
SrSe
AlO

Predict the best choice in each of the following. You may wish to review the chapter on electronic structure for relevant examples.
(a) the most metallic of the elements Al, Be, and Ba
(b) the most covalent of the compounds NaCl, CaCl2, and BeCl2
(c) the lowest first ionization energy among the elements Rb, K, and Li
(d) the smallest among Al, Al+, and Al3+
(e) the largest among Cs+, Ba2+, and Xe

answer.solution:
(a) Ba; (b) BeCl2; (c) Rb; (d) Al3+; (e) Xe.
(a) Metallic character increases down a group and decreases from left to right across a period. Barium lies at the bottom of group 2, below beryllium, and to the left of aluminum in group 13, so it loses its valence electrons most easily and is the most metallic.
(b) Beryllium is the smallest group 2 atom and has the highest ionization energies of the group, so it does not give up its electrons fully to chlorine; its compounds show covalent character, and BeCl2 is the most covalent, while NaCl and CaCl2 are ionic.
(c) First ionization energy decreases down a group as the valence electron lies farther from the nucleus and is better shielded, so rubidium, the lowest of the three in group 1, has the lowest value.
(d) All three have the same nuclear charge, 13+. Al3+ has lost all three valence electrons and keeps only 10 electrons in two shells, which the nucleus pulls in most tightly, so it is the smallest.
(e) Cs+, Ba2+ and Xe are isoelectronic, each with 54 electrons. Xenon has the lowest nuclear charge, 54+, against 55+ for Cs+ and 56+ for Ba2+, so its electrons are held least tightly and it is the largest.

exercises.prompt: Sodium chloride and strontium chloride are both white solids. How could you distinguish one from the other?

answer.solution: The possible ways of distinguishing between the two include infrared spectroscopy by comparison of known compounds, a flame test that gives the characteristic yellow color for sodium (strontium has a red flame), or comparison of their solubilities in water. At 20 °C, NaCl dissolves to the extent of $\frac{\text{35.7 g}}{\text{100 mL}}$ compared with $\frac{\text{53.8 g}}{\text{100 mL}}$ for SrCl<sub>2</sub>. Heating to 100 °C provides an easy test, since the solubility of NaCl is $\frac{\text{39.12 g}}{\text{100 mL}},$ but that of SrCl<sub>2</sub> is $\frac{\text{100.8 g}}{\text{100 mL}}.$ Density determination on a solid is sometimes difficult, but there is enough difference (2.165 g/mL NaCl and 3.052 g/mL SrCl<sub>2</sub>) that this method would be viable and perhaps the easiest and least expensive test to perform.

exercises.prompt: Does metallic tin react with HCl?

answer.solution: Yes, tin reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.

exercises.prompt: What is tin pest, also known as tin disease?

answer.solution: Tin pest, or tin disease, is the slow crumbling of tin articles to powder in cold weather, caused by the change of white tin into gray tin. Tin has two allotropes that differ in the arrangement of their atoms. White tin, the malleable metallic form, is stable above 13.2 °C; below that temperature gray tin is the more stable form, and gray tin is brittle and tends to break down to a powder. During a long cold spell white tin converts to gray tin and the article disintegrates. The change begins slowly at one spot and spreads from there, because the gray tin first formed catalyzes further change. That spreading resembles an infection in a plant or animal body, which is why the process is called tin disease or tin pest.

exercises.prompt: Compare the nature of the bonds in PbCl<sub>2</sub> to that of the bonds in PbCl<sub>4</sub>.

answer.solution: In PbCl<sub>2</sub>, the bonding is ionic, as indicated by its melting point of 501 °C. In PbCl<sub>4</sub>, the bonding is covalent, as evidenced by it being an unstable liquid at room temperature.

exercises.prompt: Is the reaction of rubidium with water more or less vigorous than that of sodium? How does the rate of reaction of magnesium compare?

answer.solution: Rubidium reacts with water more vigorously than sodium does, and magnesium reacts far more slowly than either. Reactivity of the alkali metals increases down group 1: rubidium, below sodium, is a larger atom whose single valence electron lies farther from the nucleus, so its first ionization energy is lower, it is oxidized more readily, and it releases hydrogen from water more violently. Magnesium, in the same period as sodium but in group 2, is smaller and must lose two electrons to form Mg<sup>2+</sup>, so its ionization energies are higher and it is less readily oxidized. Its surface is also passivated by a tightly adhering layer of magnesium oxycarbonate. Magnesium therefore barely reacts with cold water and reacts only slowly with hot water, giving hydrogen and a basic solution of Mg<sup>2+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> ions, as Figure 18.6 shows.
